scenes.heading: Partition Strategies
scenes.subheading: Laying out data for fast reads
scenes.narration: A partition strategy decides how a large table is physically split into folders or files so that common queries can skip the data they do not need.

scenes.heading: Principles of good partitioning
bullets: Partition on columns you filter on most
Aim for files in the hundreds of megabytes
Avoid tiny partitions and the small-file problem
Keep cardinality moderate to limit folders
scenes.narration: Partition on the columns your queries filter by most often, commonly a date, so the engine can prune whole partitions. Target file sizes in the hundreds of megabytes to balance parallelism against overhead. Avoid over-partitioning, which fragments data into many tiny files that slow every read and strain the metastore. And keep the cardinality of partition columns moderate, because a high-cardinality column like user id would create an unmanageable explosion of folders.

scenes.heading: Date partitioning vs high-cardinality
scenes.narration: Partitioning by a date column prunes the common time-range queries beautifully, keeps the number of folders manageable, and yields balanced file sizes. Partitioning directly by a high-cardinality key such as user id produces millions of tiny partitions, overwhelms the metastore with metadata, and creates the small-file problem that cripples read performance. For high-cardinality access patterns, prefer bucketing or clustering within a coarse partition rather than partitioning on the key itself.

scenes.heading: Choosing a partition scheme
scenes.narration: Start by profiling which columns your queries actually filter on and how selective they are. Choose a coarse time-based partition, such as by day or month, that matches those filters. Within each partition, bucket or cluster on secondary keys to cut down on data scanned without exploding folder counts. Schedule regular compaction to merge small files that accumulate from streaming or frequent writes. And revisit the scheme periodically, because query patterns and data volumes evolve.

scenes.heading: Beyond static partitions
bullets: Bucketing hashes rows into fixed files
Clustering and Z-ordering co-locate related rows
Hidden partitioning frees queries from layout
Iceberg and Delta support partition evolution
scenes.narration: Modern table formats move beyond rigid static partitions. Bucketing hashes rows into a fixed number of files per partition, which helps joins and high-cardinality lookups without folder explosion. Clustering and Z-ordering physically co-locate rows with similar values so data skipping is more effective. Hidden partitioning, as in Apache Iceberg, lets the engine derive partitions from a column without users having to filter on a special partition field. And formats like Iceberg and Delta even support partition evolution, so you can change the scheme without rewriting all history.

scenes.text: Partition on what you filter, keep files healthy-sized, and use bucketing for high-cardinality keys instead of exploding folders.
scenes.narration: Partition on the columns you actually filter on and keep files at a healthy size, and when you need to prune on a high-cardinality key, reach for bucketing or clustering instead of letting folders explode.
